newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African mining companies watching Zaire closely.
newsitem.headline: S.African mining companies watching Zaire closely.

text.p: South African mining companies with interests in Zaire's rich mineral potential said on Thursday they were closely watching events after Laurent Kabila's rebels seized control of the copper capital Lubumbashi.

At least three South African mining companies have submitted tenders to develop Zairean copper mines while diamond giant De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd had five diamond buying offices in Zaire and a contract with MIBA (Societe Miniere de Bakwanga) to buy its production.
De Beers pulled staff out of Kisangani in December and from the diamond capital Mbuji-Mayi a few weeks ago.

With Kabila's AFDL rebels taking control of Lubumbashi -- headquarters of state mining company Gecamines (La Generale des Carrieres et des Mines) -- on Wednesday, they now controlled most of the country's vast mineral wealth.

Zaire is viewed as potentially one of the richest mineral areas in the world yet to be fully explored. Despite growing political and economic chaos, it was Africa's fifth largest mineral producer in 1995.
Its $1.5 billion worth of mineral exports in 1995 put it behind South Africa, Gabon, Guinea and Zimbabwe.

De Beers spokesman Tom Tweedy said a resolution to Zaire's conflict would be good news. "No doubt there is a little bit of resolution on the horizon which will be good news, especially if it is peaceful," he told Reuters.

Officials of De Beers -- which controls the world diamond trade through its London-based Central Selling Organisation (CSO) -- met Kabila in Zaire at the weekend. De Beers said earlier this week it had expressed reservations about some of its properties which had been noted by the rebels.
Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd, Iscor Ltd and Gencor Ltd have submitted tenders to develop the Kolwezi tailings project in Shaba province where Lubumbashi is located.
Anglo spokeswoman Charmaine Russell said the company was watching events in Zaire closely.
"Obviously we are very interested in what is happening in Zaire. We are watching the situation," Russell added.
Gencor business development CEO David Whitehead commented: "We don't have any current investments there nor do we have any people there. But we're watching the situation with great interest."

Industry sources said that although Kabila was perceived by foreign investors to be friendly towards Western mining companies, those around him were still an unknown factor. "At least you are not hearing any reports of bloodshed," one industry source said.
